findings.note: This result is a data-availability finding, not a service-health finding. Next steps: confirm whether traces_span_metrics_calls_total exists at all and under what service_name label value for the frontend, then re-run with status_code grouping and a duration histogram quantile, adding a peer/destination label to isolate the product-catalog hop.

found.statement: The error-ratio query for frontend returned no samples in either the incident window or the preceding baseline window, so no error ratio could be computed for the service.

Because both windows are equally empty, the absence is a property of the metric series itself (span-metrics for this service name are not being produced or are named differently), not a change that coincides with the incident.
No status-code breakdown and no latency percentile data were returned; the executed query covered only the aggregate error-ratio, and the frontend->product-catalog hop was not broken out at all.

ruled_out.why: The baseline window, which precedes the incident, is equally empty. An onset-aligned telemetry loss would have shown baseline samples followed by a gap.
ruled_out.hypothesis: Frontend telemetry stopped flowing at incident onset, implying a collector or instrumentation failure triggered by the incident.

ruled_out.why: The series produced zero samples in the incident window, so it supports neither a spike nor a healthy ratio. Any claim of frontend error elevation must come from another source.
ruled_out.hypothesis: Span-metric evidence already confirms an error-rate spike at the frontend, so the frontend can be treated as the impacted tier on this basis.

ruled_out.why: The query aggregated by service_name only and returned nothing; no per-hop or per-peer dimension was ever evaluated.
ruled_out.hypothesis: The frontend->product-catalog hop can be cleared or implicated from this metric check.

verdict.reasoning: The trace sample actively excludes the obvious candidates: no callee-propagated database failure (postgresql children all under 2ms, unmarked), no failing frontend->product-catalog hop (every client span has a matching completed server child), and product-catalog's subtree is milliseconds at the end of multi-second traces [tr_d40c56f3c0c4]. What remains is a seconds-long wait accruing in the caller before the frontend server span starts, so the frontend is the service named - but whether it is slow to accept connections, briefly unreachable, or whether the load generator itself is the stall cannot be separated. The channels that would separate them all failed: product-catalog logs were never read [tr_3644135888c3, tr_4f0bef88fe0e], change history was never read and the second query's window started at onset and ran forward [tr_743335484daa], and the metric channel can support neither a spike nor health [tr_bad85b91580f, tr_e35679d06e1f]. Naming bad_config, bad_deploy or feature_flag would mean inventing a mechanism from a change log nobody successfully read.
verdict.root_cause: No root cause was established. Six of seven dispatches returned tool failures or non-existent series rather than observations: both change-history queries died on a payload parse error at the 10,000-character boundary [tr_99e786adb0bd, tr_743335484daa], both log queries were rejected by Loki with HTTP 400 due to an invalid escaped-hyphen pod regex that was never corrected [tr_3644135888c3, tr_4f0bef88fe0e], and the span-metric error ratios for product-catalog and frontend were empty in incident and baseline windows alike, meaning the series does not exist rather than having dropped at onset [tr_bad85b91580f, tr_e35679d06e1f]. The only substantive signal is the trace sample [tr_d40c56f3c0c4], and it points away from product-catalog: its server spans finish in 0.8-9.3ms with sub-2ms postgresql children and no error status, and the frontend->product-catalog hop is clean on both sides. The 0.8-2.2s user-facing latency sits almost entirely in load-generator client GET self time, with the whole frontend+product-catalog subtree occupying ~3-21ms at the tail of each trace - an un-instrumented wait on the load-generator->frontend edge. On this evidence the failing mechanism cannot be named.

alternatives.why_not: Fits the trace shape, but no frontend resource metric, log line, or pod state was ever collected; the only frontend dispatch returned a non-existent metric series [tr_e35679d06e1f].
alternatives.root_cause: frontend is saturated (threads, connections, or CPU) and callers queue before their requests are accepted, producing caller-side self time with fast downstream spans.

alternatives.why_not: Would explain 100%-self-time client spans and the lone orphan ERROR POST span, but load-generator was never dispatched against, and a critical multi-service alert is unlikely to be purely synthetic.
alternatives.root_cause: The load generator itself is the bottleneck (client-side contention or deliberate pacing), and no production service is faulty.

open_questions: What product-catalog and frontend logged at onset - the Loki query must be reissued with a valid matcher (pod=~"product-catalog-.*") before silence, exceptions, or flag text can be claimed.
What changed before 02:26:33 - both change queries failed, and one used a window starting at onset running forward, so it could not have answered even on success; re-run backward with pagination.

Where the load-generator client GET self time is actually spent: connection setup, frontend accept backlog, or load-generator-side scheduling - no frontend-side logs, resource metrics, or ingress data were gathered.

draft.title: Critical latency across six services starting at product-catalog — no cause established

sections.body:
The page came from two places at once: the load-generator and product-catalog. Severity was called critical, with six services in the blast radius and six edges crossed that we have no measurement on. The presenting symptom was user-facing latency in the range of 0.8 to 2.2 seconds, and the starting suspicion — reasonable, given the alert pair — was that product-catalog had gone bad and the frontend was inheriting it.

That suspicion did not survive the one dispatch that returned real observations. Read this record expecting a dead end: of seven dispatches, six came back as tool errors or series that do not exist, and the single good one points away from the service we started on.
sections.heading: What we saw first

sections.body:
A trace sample over the window around onset matched twenty traces and showed five of them, seventy-one spans in total. What it showed was a healthy product-catalog. Its server spans (GetProduct, ListProducts) finish in roughly 0.8ms to 9.3ms. Each one has a postgresql child completing in 0.5ms to 1.6ms, so the datastore is not holding the parent open. Where product-catalog is slowest — around seven to eight milliseconds in two traces — the time is local self time, not time waiting on the database. No product-catalog span in the sample carries an error status.

The frontend-to-product-catalog hop is clean on both sides: every frontend client span has a matching completed server child, no errors on either end. That rules out the timeout-or-aborted-call story at that hop, at least for the sampled traces.

The interesting part is where the seconds actually live. The degrading-hop breakdown attributes essentially the entire trace duration — 100% in four of the five traces — to load-generator client GET self time. The whole frontend plus product-catalog subtree occupies about 3 to 21 milliseconds, sitting at the very tail of each trace. In other words, the request spends nearly all of its life before anything we instrument starts doing work. That is an unmeasured wait on the load-generator-to-frontend edge, and we cannot see inside it.

Two caveats a future responder should carry forward. Only five of twenty matching traces were rendered and the result is marked truncated, so a rare failing product-catalog span could exist outside the sample. And the rendering surfaces no span-level error attributes at all, so even the one ERROR span we found — a load-generator client POST in a separate trace, with no product-catalog descendant and no children — cannot be read for exception detail.
sections.heading: The one piece of real evidence (T+3m)

sections.body:
We went looking for what landed before onset. Both attempts died the same way: the response payload broke the JSON parser at roughly the ten-thousandth character, mid-record. This is a failure, not an empty result — nothing about the presence or absence of changes on product-catalog was established.

The only thing the failure weakly suggests is that the log did contain a non-trivial number of entries for this service and window, since an empty set would have serialized well under the size that broke it. Treat that as a hint, not a finding.

The second attempt narrowed to configuration and flag-type records on the theory that a smaller result would parse. It failed at the same character boundary, which tells us the limit is deterministic and not driven by the breadth of record types. The lever to pull next is a shorter window, pagination, or field projection — not a type filter.

Worse, and this is the part worth remembering: the window supplied on these queries began at onset and ran twenty-four hours forward. Even on success it could not have answered what changed before onset. The question and the window were mismatched. Re-run backward.
sections.heading: Dead end: change history (two attempts)

sections.body:
Both log queries were refused by the backend with an HTTP 400. The cause is in the query we sent, not in the log store: the pod label matcher used an escaped-hyphen regex construct that the matching engine will not accept. The namespace selector and the time bounds were correct and cover onset, so neither of those is implicated.

The second attempt was issued as a correction and was not actually corrected — the same escaped-hyphen pattern went out again. Nobody caught it. That cost us the entire log channel for this investigation.

Be explicit about what this does not mean. It does not mean product-catalog was silent, crashed, or dropped its output; the request was rejected before any store lookup happened, so emptiness here carries zero information. It also does not mean the log backend is unhealthy — it answered on its cluster address with a structured client error, which requires a live server that parsed and refused the request. Permissions, retention, and tenant scoping are likewise cleared, since those surface as authorization errors or successful-but-empty responses, not a parse rejection.
sections.heading: Dead end: logs (two attempts, same broken matcher)

sections.body:
We queried error ratios for product-catalog and then for the frontend, each against both the incident window and the preceding baseline. Both returned no samples in either window.

The symmetry is the whole point. If instrumentation had died at onset we would see baseline samples followed by a gap; instead there is nothing on either side, which means the series does not exist in this backend — not produced, or produced under a different name. So this signal cannot support a claim that either service spiked errors, and equally cannot be used to pronounce either service healthy. An empty result is not a clean bill of health.

Also note the frontend query aggregated by service name only. The frontend-to-product-catalog hop was never broken out as a dimension, so nothing here clears or implicates that hop. No status-code breakdown and no latency percentiles were retrieved either.
sections.heading: Dead end: span-derived error ratios

sections.body:
No cause was established. Confidence is low and no fix class was identified. The honest summary is that the investigation spent itself on broken tooling and queries, and the single working signal reoriented the problem rather than solving it.

What we can say: product-catalog and its database were fast and error-free in the sampled traces, and the frontend-to-product-catalog hop was clean. What we cannot say: anything about what changed, anything about what either service logged, and anything from span-derived metrics at all.
sections.heading: Where this landed

sections.body:
Three threads, in rough order of payoff.

First, find out where the load-generator client GET self time actually goes. That is the only place the seconds can be hiding. Candidates are connection setup, frontend accept backlog, and load-generator-side scheduling. We gathered no frontend-side logs, no resource metrics, and no ingress data — all three are unopened.

Second, reissue the log query with a valid pod matcher. A plain pattern such as pod matching product-catalog followed by any suffix will do. Until that returns, no claim about silence, exceptions, or flag text at onset is admissible.

Third, re-run change history with a window running backward from onset, and paginate or project fields so the response stays under the size that breaks parsing. The forward-running window used here could never have answered the question asked of it.
sections.heading: Pick up here

proposal.risk: Acting now is the risk being avoided. The only substantive evidence [tr_d40c56f3c0c4] points away from product-catalog: its server spans complete in 0.8-9.3ms with sub-2ms postgresql children and no error status, and the frontend->product-catalog hop is clean on both sides. Rolling back or restarting product-catalog or frontend on this basis would destroy in-process cache, reset live connections, and likely leave the 0.8-2.2s latency untouched while consuming the incident window and corrupting the evidence trail - and a rollback has no recorded prior image tag to return to, since both change queries failed.
proposal.if_wrong: This abstention would be shown wrong if the reissued change-history query returns a deploy, image, or flag change on product-catalog or frontend inside the incident window - that would meet rollback_image or revert_config preconditions and make a targeted proposal defensible. It would also be shown wrong if corrected logs reveal a crash-loop or wedged-process signature on frontend, which would meet restart_service's precondition. Until one of those lands, any action here is a guess.
proposal.blast_radius: None from this proposal, as nothing is changed. For context on what was declined: a product-catalog action would be seen by frontend, checkout and recommendation as inbound callers; a frontend action would be seen by frontend-proxy and load-generator. Those callers remain untouched.
proposal.expected_effect: No action is proposed, so no effect is predicted. The correct next step is investigative, not remedial: reissue the Loki query with a valid matcher (pod=~"product-catalog-.*") and re-run change_history backward from 02:26:33 with pagination or a shorter window, then gather frontend-side resource/ingress data to locate the 0.8-2.2s load-generator client GET self time. None of those are actions this system may take.
